candidates.title: HOZO Hobby Knife Pairs Push-Button Blade Changes With a Fold-Out Workspace
candidates.full_text:
Small craft projects have a funny way of spreading across a table. Pieces of cardboard become a miniature building, and suddenly the knife, spare blades, and cutting mat all need their space. HOZO’s Hobby Knife design brings those essentials together, putting together a press-to-release mechanism for changing blades with a carrying case that unfolds into a cutting station. It’s a welcome design for tables with other jobs.

The case earns its place on the table even before cutting begins. Its sliding, folding arrangement opens out into a cutting station, with the attachment tray alongside the mat rather than buried underneath it. For a paper model, that puts the edges within reach while you work through walls and window openings. Even the storage gets to participate in the project.

When those components need more room, the mat slides out and unfolds further, doubling the cutting surface compared with its smaller configuration. That’s useful for a project that starts with a few pieces and gradually becomes a collection of parts waiting for assembly. You can spread out the work without separating the cutting surface from its organizer.

The knife takes a practical approach. Its hexagonal aluminum handle has flat sides that help resist rolling when you put it down, while a textured grip and raised ring give your fingers a defined holding area. The shape has something of a drafting pencil about it, a fitting reference for a tool meant to spend its time following lines and shaping details.

Of course, a project doesn’t always need the same edge from beginning to end. Switching blades here starts with a button at the back of the handle. Pressing it opens the collet, the clamp holding the blade. Exchange the attachment, then release the button to secure its replacement. The exchange drops the usual screw-tightening step from the routine.

HOZO gives the open collet a little backup. Two magnets inside the collet help retain the blade when the clamp opens, keeping it in position until you remove it. That separates two jobs neatly: the magnets help during the exchange, while the collet secures the installed blade. It’s a thoughtful detail for a tool designed around frequent attachment changes.

That change of task is where the attachment selection becomes interesting. A standard blade handles general cutting, while chisel profiles and curved edges offer different approaches to shaping details. On a miniature building, that might mean moving from cutting cardboard walls to carving a recess in a wooden trim piece. The handle stays familiar as the working end takes on a different job.

The selection extends to U- and V-gouges for carving, plus a saw and metal file for manual sawing and finishing. Those additions let the same handle follow a model component beyond its initial cut. A small groove or an edge needing refinement calls for a different attachment, rather than asking a pointed cutting blade to do every job on the table.

There are smaller considerations that make sense around delicate materials, too. The blades are hardened 420 stainless steel supplied without an oily protective coating, a welcome consideration around paper and other surfaces you’d rather keep clean. Back in the tray, magnetic slots hold attachments point-down in separate positions. Each shape has its place, so a spare blade needn’t disappear among cardboard scraps and offcuts.

The organization also accounts for what happens when a blade is spent. A one-way slot in the modular blade case provides a contained destination for used blades. It’s a modest feature, admittedly, but it gives them a place separate from fresh replacements. Changing an edge becomes part of keeping the table in order, with storage considered on both sides of a blade’s working life.

Eventually, that table might need to be a table again. The attachments return to their slots, and the cutting surface folds back into the case. The pouch-and-mat assembly is also magnetically detachable and independently replaceable. When the surface wears, that part can be changed while the organizer stays. Meanwhile, the miniature building can wait on a shelf until there’s time for its roof.

candidates.title: Knis cut a real meteorite for its $820 anniversary automatic and made just 100
candidates.full_text:
The dial on this watch isn’t painted, printed, or textured to look like stone. It’s a thin slice of Muonionalusta meteorite, a material that formed in space long before it reached Earth, cut and finished until it could sit under a sapphire crystal. Because the pattern inside the metal is natural, no two dials come out the same. Each of the 100 buyers gets a pattern nobody else has.

Knis is a small watch brand from Kyoto, and meteorite is where the whole company started. Its first watch used a meteorite dial, and five years on, the brand has gone back to that starting point for its fifth anniversary model, the KN001-MTRGLM. This version pairs the gray meteorite dial with a rose gold finish and a genuine alligator strap, and the run stops at 100 pieces worldwide. Each watch carries an engraved serial number, so the one on your wrist is numbered as part of that small run.

Plenty of watches borrow a space theme. This one uses the actual material. Knis lists the dial as Muonionalusta meteorite in its own spec table, and the brand’s anniversary note puts it plainly: the KNIS story began with a single meteorite watch. The crystalline pattern across the dial isn’t a print, so it shifts with the light in a way a textured dial can’t copy, and it won’t repeat on the next watch in the run.

The dial is signed KNIS Meteorite, and the look stays dressy rather than novelty. Rose gold markers and hands sit on top of the gray meteorite, and the alligator strap keeps the whole thing closer to a watch you’d wear with a jacket than a gadget you’d explain at parties. Though, let’s be honest, you’d still end up explaining it. The dial came from space. That’s a conversation whether you plan it or not.

The case measures 38 mm across, 46 mm from lug to lug, and 11 mm thick, and the watch weighs 73 g. That’s a compact, dress watch footprint, the kind that slides under a cuff and doesn’t announce itself by size. The case is stainless steel with a rose gold finish, the crystal is sapphire, and the strap is genuine alligator leather on a D-buckle, with a 20 mm width at the lugs.

Knis builds and assembles the watch in Japan, and it ships in the brand’s presentation box with the manual and warranty card. A one year manufacturer warranty covers it.

Inside is Miyota’s Cal. 8215, a Japanese automatic movement with manual winding and a hacking seconds hand, so the watch winds itself as you wear it and still lets you set the time precisely. The case back screws in and is see-through, which means the movement is on display every time you flip the watch over. Water resistance is rated at 10ATM, enough for rain, splashes, and everyday wear without treating the watch like it’s fragile.

There’s a nice symmetry to the spec sheet. The dial is the exotic part, and everything underneath it is proven, serviceable Japanese watchmaking. You’re not paying for an experimental movement. You’re paying for the material on top of it and for the fact that only 100 were made.

The anniversary model went on sale on November 2, 2026, at 10:00 in the morning Japan time, through the Knis official online store and the brand’s Sanjo Teramachi flagship shop in Kyoto. The price in Japan is ¥108,900 including tax. Knis’s English language store lists the watch at $820, with free DHL shipping on orders of $150 and up, and the store ships overseas. One catch to budget for: Knis notes that its prices don’t include VAT or import fees, so buyers outside Japan may owe taxes or duties on delivery depending on their country.

There’s no retailer network behind this one and no Amazon listing. If you want one, the brand’s own store is the door, and the numbered run is the limit. Once the 100 are gone, the anniversary model is done.

For a $820 watch, the buying decision here is unusually simple. The movement is a known quantity, the case size fits most wrists, and the price sits in reach of someone buying their first mechanical watch with a real story behind it. The only real questions are whether a meteorite dial is worth more to you than a conventional one, and whether you’re quick enough to claim one before the run sells through. On the first, the dial settles it the moment you see it up close. On the second, that’s up to you.

candidates.title: This Madrid restaurant built a greenhouse to sell the vegetables it cooks with
candidates.full_text:
I’ll admit it, I have never once looked at a supermarket tomato and wondered where it grew up. Filandón, a restaurant tucked into the woods of El Pardo on the edge of Madrid, wants to fix that habit with architecture. At its entrance sits a glass greenhouse used as a farm shop, selling the vegetables the kitchen cooks with. Every crate of potatoes and string of dried chilies comes from the restaurant’s own farm. You can eat the menu, then buy the menu, which is honestly a great business model.

Barcelona-based Trenchs Studio designed the structure, borrowing its silhouette from the classic European glasshouse, with an aluminum frame, pitched glass roof, and decorative cresting along the ridge. Founder Ricard Trenchs has spent the better part of two decades designing restaurant interiors. Here, custom bronze pedestals outside hold baskets of produce and can be rearranged as the seasons change. Inside, a wood-and-stone table serves as a counter and guides shoppers through the space without a single interior wall. The produce travels from Granja de los Monjes, the owners’ organic farm in northwestern Spain’s El Bierzo region.

Designer: Trenchs Studio (Ricard Trenchs)

Filandón is an old Leonese word for the winter gatherings when villagers sat around the fire to spin thread and swap stories. It comes from the Latin filum, meaning thread, and León’s writers still stage literary filandones in its honor. The restaurant’s connection to León extends to the García Azpiroz family behind it, whose roots trace back to the muleteers of the region’s Maragatería area. Diners can now walk out with the same tomatoes and peppers that landed on their plates an hour earlier. Doggy bags have officially been upgraded.

The produce comes from Granja de los Monjes, roughly 240 miles (385 km) northwest of Madrid by road. The name translates to “the monks’ farm.” The family bought Granja de Santullano, a 12th-century monastic grange in San Esteban de Valdueza long tied to farming and winemaking, and is regenerating about 148 acres (60 hectares) there. Restoration crews even found an 18th-century wine cellar hidden beneath the old buildings, which is the most Spanish renovation surprise imaginable. Tomatoes, potatoes, piparra peppers, artichokes, lettuce, and asparagus grow there organically. The harvest supplies the group’s Madrid restaurants, and the greenhouse lets diners carry some of it home.

The group in question is Pescaderías Coruñesas, founded in A Coruña in 1911 to bring seafood to Madrid. It runs El Pescador, O’Pazo, and Filandón, and in 2021 it rescued Lhardy, a Madrid institution dating to 1839, from insolvency. The greenhouse shelves also carry Pescaderías Coruñesas preserves alongside Lhardy’s liqueurs. Petersham Nurseries in London combines a greenhouse, restaurant, and store on one property, while Amsterdam’s De Kas grows produce in the same glasshouse where you eat. At Filandón, the glasshouse is the shop, while the growing happens 240 miles away.

The silhouette recalls the 19th-century European glasshouse, with its cast-iron frame and plate glass built to shelter exotic plants. Here, the frame is slim aluminum in a dark olive finish that blends with the trees of Monte de El Pardo, one of Europe’s best-preserved Mediterranean forests. Gooseneck lamps glow above the doors, and dried chili ristras hang inside the frame. The bronze pedestals out front display what’s for sale before you reach the door. Glass has one big weakness in Madrid, though, and it’s the sun.

Trenchs addressed that with alicantina blinds, the wooden slats strung on cord that hang outside windows across Alicante, Valencia, and Murcia. They roll up on a simple pulley, shade the glass, and let air slip between the slats, all without a motor. Architects around Spain have been reviving them as a low-tech way to limit heat gain. Here, olive-green wooden blinds stretch across the greenhouse roof. They can be adjusted throughout the day and across the seasons to help keep the shop usable year-round.

A dark herringbone timber floor runs through the interior, and an oak unit in a warm tobacco tone lines the back wall, displaying preserves and bottles under focused lighting. Ceramic lamps with linen shades sit on the stone-topped table like it’s someone’s living room. The effect is a jewelry store for vegetables, with tomatoes getting the spotlight usually reserved for watches. Trenchs once described the challenge of an all-glass Barcelona restaurant he designed
